content.title: About
content.content: Peach pie is a baked dessert consisting of a tender crust filled with fresh or canned peach slices sweetened with sugar and flavored with cinnamon. The crust can be shortcrust, flaky, or yeasted, and the filling often includes a splash of lemon juice to balance the sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peaches belong to the Rosaceae family and are close relatives of apricots, plums, and cherries.
The tradition of making peach pie began in Europe in the 19th century when improved transport made peaches widely available.
In the United States, peach pie is sometimes served at Thanksgiving as an alternative to apple pie.
There are many crust variations, from classic shortcrust to gluten‑free almond‑flour bases.
Peaches are rich in vitamin C and beta‑carotene, making the filling both tasty and nutritious.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen production, important for skin and blood vessels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Peaches provide beta‑carotene and flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in sodium
items.content: Peach pie typically contains little added salt, which is beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the crust and fruit offers a quick source of energy.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The sweetened filling can raise blood glucose levels; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional crusts contain wheat flour, which may be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Butter, sugar, and crust make the pie relatively high in calories, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: If margarine or pre‑made crusts are used, they may contain trans fats, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve peach pie warm, often with whipped cream, vanilla ice cream, or a dollop of custard. Slice into portions and keep refrigerated for up to 3 days. For a brighter flavor, add a touch of lemon zest to the filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Allow the pie to cool completely, then cover tightly with plastic wrap or place in an airtight container. Store in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven before serving.

potato-baked-peel-not-eaten-with-butter.title: Potato, baked, peel not eaten, with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato with the peel removed and served with butter is a popular side dish in many cuisines worldwide. Baking retains most of the potato's nutrients, and the added butter enhances flavor while improving the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baking caramelizes the natural sugars in potatoes, intensifying their aroma.
Potato skins contain more fiber and vitamins, but they are discarded in this preparation.
Serving baked potatoes with butter is a tradition in Russian, German, and American kitchens.
Potatoes are one of the most consumed root vegetables globally, with annual production exceeding 350 million tonnes.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Baked potatoes are high in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Although some vitamin C is lost during cooking, baked potatoes still provide a notable amount of this antioxidant.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes supply slowly digestible carbs that provide sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins with butter
items.content: Adding butter helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K present in small amounts in the potato.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Even without the skin, the flesh contains dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: High calorie content with excess butter
items.content: Using too much butter can increase the dish's calorie density and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Baked potatoes have a high glycemic index, which may cause rapid blood sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Butter allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to the type of oil or butter used in preparation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the baked potato hot, drizzled with butter or melted butter. It can be added to salads, used as a base for casseroles, or enjoyed simply as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked baked potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to retain a pleasant texture.

rice-white-with-corn-fat-added.title: White Rice with Corn and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with corn and added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected white rice, toasted together with corn kernels and enriched with vegetable oil. It has a mild flavor, a hint of corn sweetness, and a smooth, buttery texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑corn combination increases carbohydrate content, making the dish more filling.
Added vegetable fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin E.
The product is often used in children’s meals and athletes’ diets for quick energy replenishment.
The white rice is polished, reducing fiber but making it easier to digest.
Corn gives the mix a characteristic golden color and a subtle aromatic note.

items.title: Rapid energy source
items.content: High carbohydrate content provides a quick glucose boost, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Supports nervous system
items.content: Rice contains vitamin B1 (thiamine), which is essential for nerve impulse transmission.

items.title: Improves vitamin absorption
items.content: Vegetable fat helps the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins like vitamin E and K more efficiently.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Polished white rice is gentle on the stomach, making the product suitable for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Corn is rich in carotenoids, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The product can raise blood sugar quickly, so individuals with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to the corn component.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Added oil increases caloric density, which is important for weight management.

items.title: Low fiber
items.content: Polished rice provides little dietary fiber, so it does not replace whole‑grain sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in the microwave or on the stovetop, add it to soups, stews, or use as a side dish for meat and fish. It also works as a quick snack when paired with vegetables or a sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in a sealed package. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container and use within 2‑3 days. For longer storage, keep refrigerated for up to 1 week.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice with raisins is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of cooked rice mixed with dried raisins. It is commonly used in baby foods, diet meals, and as a quick snack. Rice provides energy, while raisins add natural sweetness and a modest amount of vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑raisin combination is traditional in many cuisines, including Indian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean.
Raisins retain some antioxidants, such as polyphenols, even after drying.
Rice with raisins is often served in kindergartens as part of a balanced diet.
Some recipes include spices like cinnamon or cardamom to enhance flavor.
The product can be stored dry and only requires hot water to rehydrate.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies easily digestible carbs for quick energy.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Raisins provide iron, which helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber from raisins supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice contains B1 and B3 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in raisins have antioxidant activity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the overall sugar level, so people with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to rice.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose products with quality certifications to minimize pesticide exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat: open the pack and, if desired, add hot water or milk. It can be used as a filling for pancakes, mixed into yogurt, oatmeal, or desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. Avoid direct sunlight for long‑term storage. The shelf life is indicated on the packaging.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate soy milk is a beverage made from soybeans, enriched with cocoa butter and sugar. It has a smooth, creamy taste with a distinct chocolate note and is often used as a dairy‑free alternative for those avoiding lactose or animal protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Commercial soy milk production began in Japan in the early 1920s.
The chocolate flavor is achieved by adding cocoa butter, not just cocoa powder, for a richer mouthfeel.
Soybeans are rich in isoflavones, which may have beneficial effects on hormonal balance.
In some countries, chocolate soy milk is marketed as a "kids' drink" and is common in school cafeterias.
Unlike cow's milk, soy milk naturally contains no lactose.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of soy milk provides about 7 g of protein, making it a solid alternative to animal proteins.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The chocolate version typically contains less saturated fat than whole cow's milk.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12 (fortified)
items.content: Many brands fortify soy milk with vitamin B12, important for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Isoflavones may support cardiovascular health and bone density.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Soy fiber helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy proteins.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Chocolate varieties are often sweetened, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Genetically modified soybeans
items.content: The majority of soybeans worldwide are GMO; choose "non‑GMO" labeled products if preferred.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Soy contains phytates that can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate soy milk can be enjoyed cold, added to smoothies, used in oatmeal, coffee, or baked goods. It pairs well with bananas, berries, and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Refrigerate after opening and consume within 5‑7 days. Unopened cartons should be stored in a cool, dry place away from direct light.
